# A first 100 km sportive or long ride: a 12-week plan (active start)

*Generated by the Don't Die Retired guidance engine on 1 November 2026 from 34 sourced statements. Draft for review: not yet checked by a coach, physiotherapist or doctor.*

## The challenge

100 km (62 miles) in the saddle in a day, often with hills and food stops along the way. [1, 2]

**Before this plan:** If you cannot yet ride for an hour comfortably, start with British Cycling's eight-week Sofa to 50km plan, which builds from three short rides a week to a 50 km ride. [3, 4, 5]

## Before you start

- If you have a health condition or are worried about your health, speak to your GP (family doctor) before you start training. [4, 6]
- Start from your current level and build up gradually; repeating a week is fine and is part of the plan, not a failure. [3, 4, 5]

## How the plan works

- Do most of your training at an easy, conversational effort, about 2 to 3 out of 10, where you could hold a full conversation. Keep a small share for harder work. [7, 8, 9, 10]
- Increase your training a little at a time. Big week-to-week jumps (more than about 30 per cent) were linked with more overuse injuries in a study of 874 new runners; the familiar 10 per cent rule is a sensible cap but is not firmly proven. [4, 11, 12]
- Every third or fourth week, ease back on volume to let your body absorb the work before building again; older runners and people under other stress may do best with every third week. [9, 13]
- Build one long session a week at an easy effort, growing towards the length and duration of the challenge itself. [2, 9]
- Know the real demands of your challenge (distance, total climb, time on your feet, altitude) and make sure your plan builds towards them. [1, 2]
- Plan rest days into every week, and take an easier day when your legs are heavy. [4, 9, 14]
- Do strength exercises for the whole body on at least two days a week. In trials, strength training cut sports injuries to about a third. [2, 3, 5, 15]
- In the final two weeks, cut your training volume by roughly 40 to 60 per cent while keeping the same number of sessions and some of the same effort, so you arrive fresh. [9, 16, 17, 18]
- Build one long ride a week at an easy pace, growing gradually towards the distance of the event; Cycling UK's plan for a 100 km ride takes the long ride from 15 to 25 km up to 90 to 100 km over nine weeks. [10, 19]

## Week by week

Rest on Mondays and Fridays. Strength and balance (about 30 minutes, routine below) on Wednesdays and Sundays. Why each part is there, and what changes each week, follows the table. The Saturday long ride is the key session: at an easy, conversational pace, eating and drinking as you go.

| 1 | easy ride, 45 min | easy ride, 45 min | 40 km (25 miles) |  |
| 2 | easy ride, 45 min | easy ride, 45 min | 46 km (29 miles) |  |
| 3 | easy ride, 45 min | easy ride, 45 min | 37 km (23 miles) | easier week |

| 5 | easy ride, 45 min | easy ride, 45 min | 62 km (38 miles) |  |
| 6 | easy ride, 45 min | easy ride, 45 min | 49 km (31 miles) | easier week |

| 10 | easy ride, 45 min | easy ride, 45 min | 95 km (59 miles) |  |

## What each part of the plan is for

- **The Saturday long ride.** The long session prepares you for the length of the day itself. Its pace does not matter; covering the time or distance does, so keep it at a conversational effort. [1, 2, 9]
- **The easy rides.** Easy sessions add fitness without leaving you too tired for the long session. Top endurance athletes do about four in five of their sessions at this low effort. [7, 8]
- **Strength and balance.** Strength and balance work is what keeps you in one piece. In trials it cut sports injuries to about a third, it is part of the official guidance for everyone on at least two days a week, and core and balance work helps on rough ground. [2, 3, 15]
- **Rest days.** Rest days are when your body recovers from the work and adapts to it. The NHS's beginner running plan puts a rest day between every run. [4, 13]
- **Easier weeks.** An easier week every third week lets the tiredness of the previous weeks clear, so your fitness can rebound before you build again. [9, 13]
- **The taper.** Cutting back in the final weeks lets your muscles recover and your body refuel, so you arrive fresh rather than tired. In research, a two-week taper improved performance. [16, 17]

## Each week, and why

**Week 1: setting the pattern.**

- Five sessions and two rest days. The long ride starts at 40 km (25 miles).
- Why the long session: it gets you used to the hours you will spend out on the day; pace does not matter [1, 2, 9]
- Tuesday's easy ride: it adds fitness while leaving you fresh for the long session [7, 8]
- Strength and balance, Wednesday and Sunday: it protects you from injury (about a third of the injuries in trials) and keeps you steady on rough ground [2, 3, 15]
- Rest on Monday and Friday: your body recovers and adapts on the days you rest, not the days you train [4, 13]

**Week 2: building.**

- The long ride grows to 46 km (29 miles), up from 40 km (25 miles) in your last full week.
- Why only this much more: big jumps from one week to the next are linked with overuse injuries. [4, 11, 12]
- Strength and balance, Wednesday and Sunday: it protects you from injury (about a third of the injuries in trials) and keeps you steady on rough ground [2, 3, 15]

**Week 3: an easier week.**

- The long ride eases back to 37 km (23 miles).
- Why ease off: it lets the last two weeks' tiredness clear so your fitness can catch up [9, 13]
- Rest on Monday and Friday: your body recovers and adapts on the days you rest, not the days you train [4, 13]

**Week 4: building.**

- The long ride grows to 53 km (33 miles), up from 46 km (29 miles) in your last full week.
- Why the long session: it gets you used to the hours you will spend out on the day; pace does not matter [1, 2, 9]
- Tuesday's easy ride: it adds fitness while leaving you fresh for the long session [7, 8]

**Week 5: building.**

- The long ride grows to 62 km (38 miles), up from 53 km (33 miles) in your last full week.
- Why only this much more: big jumps from one week to the next are linked with overuse injuries. [4, 11, 12]
- Strength and balance, Wednesday and Sunday: it protects you from injury (about a third of the injuries in trials) and keeps you steady on rough ground [2, 3, 15]

**Week 6: an easier week.**

- The long ride eases back to 49 km (31 miles).
- Why ease off: it lets the last two weeks' tiredness clear so your fitness can catch up [9, 13]
- Rest on Monday and Friday: your body recovers and adapts on the days you rest, not the days you train [4, 13]

**Week 7: building.**

- The long ride grows to 71 km (44 miles), up from 62 km (38 miles) in your last full week.
- Why the long session: it gets you used to the hours you will spend out on the day; pace does not matter [1, 2, 9]
- Tuesday's easy ride: it adds fitness while leaving you fresh for the long session [7, 8]

**Week 8: building.**

- The long ride grows to 82 km (51 miles), up from 71 km (44 miles) in your last full week.
- Why only this much more: big jumps from one week to the next are linked with overuse injuries. [4, 11, 12]
- Strength and balance, Wednesday and Sunday: it protects you from injury (about a third of the injuries in trials) and keeps you steady on rough ground [2, 3, 15]

**Week 9: an easier week.**

- The long ride eases back to 66 km (41 miles).
- Why ease off: it lets the last two weeks' tiredness clear so your fitness can catch up [9, 13]
- Rest on Monday and Friday: your body recovers and adapts on the days you rest, not the days you train [4, 13]

**Week 10: your biggest week.**

- Your longest long ride of the plan, 95 km (59 miles), as close to the real day as training gets.
- Why the long session: it gets you used to the hours you will spend out on the day; pace does not matter [1, 2, 9]
- Tuesday's easy ride: it adds fitness while leaving you fresh for the long session [7, 8]

**Week 11: taper.**

- The long ride drops to 57 km (35 miles), but you keep every session.
- Why less now: your muscles recover and your body refuels, so you arrive fresh [16, 17]
- Tuesday's easy ride: it adds fitness while leaving you fresh for the long session [7, 8]
- Keep both strength sessions but make them lighter: same sessions, less of each.
- Rest on Monday and Friday: your body recovers and adapts on the days you rest, not the days you train [4, 13]

**Week 12: the challenge.**

- Two short, easy outings early in the week and plenty of rest: your muscles recover and your body refuels, so you arrive fresh [16, 17]
- No strength sessions this week; arrive rested.


## Looking after your body

- Include balance work; for older adults the official guidance pairs it with strength on two days a week, and balance (proprioception) training also reduced injuries in trials. [3, 5, 15]
- Stretch after a long day if it feels good, but do not rely on stretching to prevent injury; trials found it made no difference, unlike strength and balance work. [2, 15]
- Weight-bearing activity such as walking and running helps keep bones strong. [3]
- Keep a regular sleep routine through training; good sleep is part of recovery, and on multi-day trips a warm enough sleeping bag and mat matter more than people expect. [14, 17]
- If you miss a session, do not worry about it; carry on with the plan, or repeat a week if you need to. [4, 17]

**Strength and balance routine (twice a week).** Squats, lunges, a core exercise such as a plank, and a balance exercise such as standing on one leg. Start with your own body weight, two sets of 8 to 12 slow repetitions, and add load only when that feels easy. [2, 3, 5, 15]

## Fuel, drink and feet

- On long days eat regularly on the move, a little and often from a variety of foods, rather than one big meal before you start. [2, 20]
- Use your long sessions to practise exactly what you will eat and drink on the day, building up gradually so your stomach gets used to it. Nothing new on the day. [17, 20]
- On long rides eat something every 20 to 30 minutes, and carry enough food and drink for the whole ride rather than relying on finding a shop. [10, 19]

## On the day

- Start slower than you think you need to; early miles feel easy and are where most people overdo it. [7, 17]
- Make sure your bike is the right size, comfortable and working, check tyres, brakes and chain before each ride, and carry a spare inner tube, repair kit and pump. [10, 19]
- Start every ride at an easy pace for about five minutes to warm up, and finish with five to ten minutes of slower riding. [10]

## Safety

- Drink when you are thirsty rather than to a schedule. Drinking far more than you need can dilute the body's sodium, which can be dangerous; it affects walkers and recreational exercisers as well as racers. [21]
- Call 999 (911 in the US) for tight or squeezing chest pain, pain spreading to the arms, neck or jaw, severe breathlessness, or if someone collapses. Do not drive yourself to hospital. [22]
- Stop if something does not feel right, and get it checked rather than training through it. [4, 17]
